I want to talk about a high-level overview for why we want to reduce the dimension. Dimensionality reduction is a way to process your features, your input data. It's important for us to reduce the dimension. Mathematically, reducing dimension means having some kind of mapping where you want to reduce your dataset from a higher dimension to a smaller dimension. If you have some kind of real number N, you want to map it to a real number M, where M is smaller than N.

If you realize in the Kaggle data provided, you are given a huge number of input features. When you start to do more feature engineering, your feature sets can grow beyond 77 features. Who has more, actually? Who ended up with more? Just give me a show of hands. Who explored and ended up with more than the given? Nobody. Okay, some. You realize that when you start to engineer features, you have the... anyway, you are too competitive. The whole idea here is that sometimes you do have a lot of input data, and I will share some motivations on why it's important. Today, we will talk mainly about one technique, Principal Component Analysis, which is a linear transformation. I will give resources for t-SNE but will focus mainly on PCA. These techniques, these algorithms, this transformation, basically aim to find some kind of mapping where you are transforming your data from a higher dimension to a smaller dimension.

From an intuition perspective, when your number of features increases, you need a larger number of data to generalize the input space. I will show an illustration later to show that when you think about higher dimensions, the number of data required to fill the data space increases exponentially. If you have too many features, some might be noise. This falls into feature selection. Dimensionality reduction aims to project transformations from a higher dimensional space to a smaller dimensional space, allowing you to select or tweak knobs to reduce noise.

The last thing, which is also true, is that as human beings, you can only visualize three dimensions. If anyone can visualize more than three, please let me know. Typically, if you have higher dimensional data, you want to project them to a smaller dimension so you can visualize, either in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space. Beyond that, as human beings, we cannot interpret higher dimensions. You want to perform some kind of transformation, with constraints to maintain the data's relationship without changing it too much, and visualize them in two-dimensional space.

If you imagine one of the algorithms we taught last week, from a KNN perspective, if you have one single dimension, let's say you only need 5 blocks of data to represent a certain data space. If I think about this data in two dimensions, it becomes 5 times 5, which is 25. If I think about this in three-dimensional space, the number of data points becomes 5 to the power of 3. The idea is that when you think about higher dimensions, you essentially need much more data to represent the data space. In KNN, this grows exponentially. For every dimension you add, you are not increasing linearly. The number of data to best represent this same space increases exponentially. That is the intuition for the curse of dimensionality.

One technique we will spend time talking about today is Principal Component Analysis, a very common linear transformation. Because it's linear, there are some assumptions. The idea is that we want to project this data, through a linear transformation, into some kind of linear combination of features. From a data perspective, the projection will project your data in the direction that maximizes the variance. It's the greatest variance. The intuition for wanting variance is that we want to spread the data. If we can spread the data out maximally, with a larger spread, then we can capture the necessary information from the data itself.

From a graphical perspective, if I have a graph and I want to project the data, let's say this is the new data I'm projecting. If the final projection is able to, this is the component I projected. Imagine my data is 10 dimensions. If I project them to 2 dimensions, and this is the first component I'm projecting my data to, and if I'm able to have a good projection such that the data is well spread out, then I can segregate this data and capture all the information to separate it. That's the idea.

One more characteristic of PCA is that each of the components are orthogonal. Orthogonal just looks something like that. This is the second component. The idea is that you always want your new projection to be smaller than your current projection. If you have 10 features in 10 dimensions, I will always want to find a projection that is less than 10. PCA projects them linearly such that the first component has the maximum variance.

If you look at the first component and think about maximum variance, what does it remind you of? It's very similar to OLS. Coincidentally, the component that maximizes the maximum variance also reduces the sum of squares. There's a relation very similar to linear regression.

The intuition to take away is that you want your component. You want to find a mapping where PCA maps the data from N dimension to M dimension, where you select M to be smaller than your original dimension. These M components, or this M number of projections, the first component will always be the one that has the maximum, the largest variance, to explain the data. The larger the variance, the more the component can spread out the data, the better it is, because it captures more information. If I can separate them nicely, as far as possible, this new representation of the data. If I can separate them very far away, it means I can capture the information needed. If all the data is clumped up together, I don't have enough context to separate them. You want to find features that can distinguish each data point as far as possible. Think about it from your HDB flat data prediction. If your X values make all the data cluttered together, it's not useful. I want to find information that can spread them out as far as possible, able to distinguish them. High variance is a good thing. We want to find a mapping that maximizes the variance.

PCA is a linear transformation, which means it has underlying assumptions that the components have some kind of linear relationship. If your features are non-linear in their relationship, then PCA will not work out. I will show you how to see this later. Any questions?

Keywords: Principal Component Analysis, PCA, linear transformation, maximize variance, orthogonal components, OLS, linear regression, feature projection, linear relationship, data spread

chunk_text:
The goal is for data points to be very spread out after projection, not clumped together. When I say maximum variance, I mean I want all the dots to be spread out far apart after the transformation. If you transform data and it's all clumped up, that's a bad projection because you're not capturing enough information to differentiate points. If you capture enough information, you can group everybody separately. That's what I mean by maximum variance. While PCA does have a reconstruction error it tries to minimize, the key takeaway is that you want to find a new representation of your data where the first component has the best variance, spreading the data out as far as possible. You want your features to have this spread because it allows your model to classify or group them into different things. For example, if you're inputting features like house location, you want a component that spreads the data out very far apart from each other, like houses in Orchard versus houses in Jurong versus houses in Sembawang.

Keywords: pca, maximum variance, data spread, projection, differentiation, reconstruction error, feature spread, house location example

The idea is that if I want to make some kind of prediction, having things that allows me to group and cut them is very important. It means that the input feature is important. Let's say, for example, in the case of an HDB flat, your goal is to predict different buckets of flats. Maybe you have Y1, Y2, Y3, and Y4. A good feature, by definition, is one that allows you to separate all of them. For example, if you think that a good indicator to predict a house is the location, then the location variable must be able to split the data into different partitions. If your intuition is that the location matters, then having this variable should split my data out into different groups. A useless variable is one where you put in the variable, it doesn't tell me anything; it just tells me everybody is still the same. That's by definition useless. There's no information for me. The intuition here is that a good variable, a good X, must be one that helps you cut them nicely. Of course, cut them in a way where all of them are able to group into different, similar values. The intuition here is that being able to split data up is a good thing, not a bad thing. Consider the location, for example.
